transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Recording link: (redacted)
Shared artifacts: Mistral-Redwood-kv-lab-deck.pdf, eviction-trace-20260928.csv, benchmark-matrix.xlsx

Summary:
Short root-cause lab focused on repeated KV spillover during long-context streaming. Customer reporting bursts where KV cache evicts warm prefixes, causing paging to disk and tail latency spikes. Redwood AE+SE to reproduce with trace, validate prefetch heuristics, and propose config changes (batching, kv-ttl, routing).

Topics covered:
- KV cache eviction patterns and prefix locality
- Paging/spill behavior under mixed short/long context workloads
- Impact of batching and continuous prefetching on latency and throughput
- Quantization tradeoffs when memory pressure increases
- VPC/on-prem constraints for pilot and telemetry collection

Transcript body:
[00:00] Camila Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Camila, AE on the Redwood platform. Quick intro, then I'll hand off to Ravi for the deep dive.
[00:12] Daniel Kim: Hi, Daniel from Mistral platform team. We're seeing periodic tail latency spikes tied to KV cache spill events.
[00:18] Camila Ortiz: Yep, that's what we want to drill into, thanks. Ravi, over to you.
[00:23] Ravi Patel: Thanks. Hi all. I'll run through the architecture we think is in play, then we'll map to your trace. Apologies in advance, I might say "kayvee" instead of KV, and sometimes product names get munged.
[00:36] (laughter)
[00:39] Ravi Patel: So high level, our serving runtime keeps a per-worker KV cache for autoregressive decoding. It's a hot-prefix first cache, continuous batching, and it has a spill-to-disk mechanism when memory crosses the threshold. On mixed workloads where long-context requests show up interleaved with short sessions, we sometimes see prefix churn which can evict warm keys.
[01:05] Tomoko Sato: Right, that's what we're observing. We have sessions that go to 35k tokens occasionally, but most calls are sub-1k. The pattern seems to evict the short-session prefixes after a long-context arrives, then the short calls suffer while disk pages are refilled.
[01:23] Ravi Patel: Exactly. Two things to confirm from your trace: are long-context requests multiplexed onto the same worker pools as short ones, and what's the sequence length distribution entro— I mean distribution?
[01:36] Daniel Kim: They're all routed by same route currently. We haven't separated them. Sequence histogram is in the CSV we shared; it's heavy tail with 2.4% over 20k tokens.
[01:46] Ravi Patel: Great. That explains the intermittent memory pressure. The runtime uses an LRU-like eviction but with prefix affinity heuristics. When a long request consumes KV capacity, it may cause eviction of prefixes that are actually hot for short calls later.
[02:02] Lina Alvarez: Is there a mechanism to pin prefixes for critical customers or session affinity?
[02:08] Ravi Patel: We support prefix pinning in Dedicated and Private with a config called prefix_preserve_ratio, but it's off by default for hosted routes to avoid undermining pool utilization. For your case, pinning critical prefixes or creating a route split could help.
[02:27] Daniel Kim: We tried pinning heuristics client-side but didn't have visibility into actual evictions. The trace shows repeated re-fetches for the same prefixes.
[02:36] Ravi Patel: We'll need to correlate your fetch IDs with our KV telemetry. If you can share the trace with request IDs that map to our logs, I can run an eviction replay.
[02:46] Camila Ortiz: Quick note — we'll also send our KV telemetry schema so your team can map fields.
[02:53] Tomoko Sato: One question: when the KV spills to disk, is that per-worker ephemeral disk or a network-backed page store?
[03:01] Ravi Patel: For hosted we use ephemeral local NVMe on the instance; in Dedicated and Private we can optionally configure networked blob stores for larger spill capacity. The main penalty is read-amplification and latency for page-in.
[03:16] (small crosstalk)
[03:18] Daniel Kim: In our case, the spikes are 700-1200ms p95 during refill windows, which matches a disk page-in profile.
[03:27] Ravi Patel: Makes sense. Two levers: reduce frequency of evictions (increase memory footprint or change eviction thresholds), or reduce page-in impact (prefetch, async background prefetching, smaller page sizes).
[03:40] Lina Alvarez: We want to avoid just throwing GPUs at this. Any config changes that are cost-neutral?
[03:46] Ravi Patel: Yes. A few low-cost configs:
- Increase kv-ttl to keep prefixes longer (if memory allows)
- Set aggressive prefix reuse detection window so recent prefixes are less likely to be evicted
- Turn on adaptive prefetch for sessions with high reuse 
These don't require more hardware, just tuning, though they can slightly increase memory usage.
[04:06] Daniel Kim: What's the tradeoff for batching? We thought increasing batch windows would help but it seemed to worsen latency in some periods.
[04:14] Ravi Patel: Batching helps amortize cost across tokens but increases per-request latency if windows are big. Also, batching interacts with KV because larger batches hold onto KV positions longer; that can increase memory residence time, paradoxically reducing eviction, but if a long-context holds many KV entries then it can also cause eviction by occupying space. It's workload dependent.
[04:36] Tomoko Sato: So a small batching window could reduce the time a long-context holds keys and help?
[04:41] Ravi Patel: Potentially. Another approach is route-based throttling: send long-contexts to a worker pool with larger memory per worker or higher prefix_preserve_ratio.
[04:52] Daniel Kim: What about quantization? We're using int8 models in prod; will quantization increase or decrease memory pressure?
[04:59] Ravi Patel: Quant reduces model weights footprint, but KV entries are usually float32 activations in the cache. We support compressed KV serialization (mixed precision) which can cut KV size ~2x but with a small accuracy delta. For you, compressed KV + slightly higher kv-ttl could be a win.
[05:18] Camila Ortiz: Quick check — are you doing streaming output for these sessions?
[05:22] Daniel Kim: Yes, streaming enabled. We think streaming plus long contexts may be holding the KV longer.
[05:27] Ravi Patel: Streaming causes incremental prefix growth; combined with long contexts it exacerbates memory residency. We can instrument to show per-request KV life span.
[05:36] (pause)
[05:40] Ravi Patel: Now let's step through your specific trace. I pulled an example where a long request arrives at 03:14:22 UTC and we see a cascade of evictions 8s later.
[05:51] Lina Alvarez: That matches our alerting window — we saw the spike ~10s after large job started.
[05:57] Ravi Patel: In the trace, the long job streamed tokens for ~22s which corresponds to approx 18k tokens. The cache ramped and hit spill threshold. Then short sessions that started within 30s saw p95 blow up.
[06:11] Daniel Kim: Is the 30s window tunable?
[06:14] Ravi Patel: Yes, parameters: kv-eviction-grace (defaults 30s) and kv-spill-threshold (percent of worker mem). We generally tune kv-eviction-grace to match session reuse patterns; if you have short sessions returning within 20-40s, increase the grace to avoid premature eviction.
[06:33] Tomoko Sato: Any negative side effects to increasing grace broadly?
[06:36] Ravi Patel: Higher grace increases memory residency and raises probability of spill under heavy long-context load. It's a balancing act. For mixed loads we recommend split routing first.
[06:46] Daniel Kim: How feasible is split routing in hosted? Would we need a separate model variant?
[06:51] Ravi Patel: No need for model variant; create two routes mapping to the same model but different runtime config (kv-preserve, worker_size). It's supported and we can do a canary for a subset of traffic.
[07:05] Lina Alvarez: We'll likely try split routing: short-route optimized for low-latency (<1k tokens) and long-route for heavy contexts. What's involved to test?
[07:13] Ravi Patel: We'll propose a pilot plan: 1) run eviction replay against your trace to simulate behavior under split routing and different kv parameters; 2) recommend config changes; 3) run a small A/B canary with 5-10% traffic.
[07:26] Camila Ortiz: Adding: we'll supply recommended YAML snippets for route configs.
[07:30] Daniel Kim: Great. Two other notes from our security team: audit logs and KMS policy needs — will that telemetry capture be PII-free?
[07:38] Camila Ortiz: Yes, telemetry is sanitized, we only ask for request IDs and token counts. For Private deployment, logs can stay in your VPC and integrate with your KMS.
[07:48] Tomoko Sato: For the eviction replay, can you also vary page size and prefetch window?
[07:53] Ravi Patel: Absolutely. We'll sweep kv-page-size (default 4MB) and prefetch-window (default 3) across values. We'll include metrics: p50/p95 latency, disk IOPS, cache hit ratio, and memory residency.
[08:06] (background typing)
[08:10] Daniel Kim: Any gotchas with our on-prem plans? We're evaluating Private for data residency.
[08:15] Ravi Patel: On-prem introduces network topology differences — if spill uses network blob store, page-in latency can be higher. Also hardware differences (NVMe vs SAN) change behavior. We'll recommend local NVMe for page store for low-latency paging.
[08:28] Lina Alvarez: Good to know. Our SRE prefers predictable latency, so Dedicated with pinned workers might be ideal long-term.
[08:36] Ravi Patel: That's a common path: start with hosted tweaks, pilot split routing, then move to Dedicated with configured worker sizes if needed.
[08:44] Daniel Kim: Can we get a sample config for prefix pinning? You mentioned prefix_preserve_ratio earlier.
[08:50] Ravi Patel: Yes — example: prefix_preserve_ratio: 0.2 (means top 20% prefixes are preserved), kv-eviction-grace: 45s. We'll send a few sample combos and simulated results.
[09:02] Camila Ortiz: Quick practical: we can also enable a short-term workaround where we throttle concurrent long-context sessions during peak times. Not ideal but reduces evictions.
[09:12] Tomoko Sato: Might be acceptable as temporary.
[09:15] Daniel Kim: One more: we do token-level caching on our side at the gateway; are there interactions?
[09:20] Ravi Patel: If you cache at gateway and skip calls often, it reduces load and reduces KV churn. However, partial misses still show up; we should model gateway cache hit rates in the replay.
[09:31] (brief pause)
[09:34] Ravi Patel: Ok, let's talk instrumentation — we need three things from you: request IDs, approximate sequence lengths, and a 24h traffic sample. Attach those to the trace and we'll run the replay.
[09:45] Daniel Kim: We'll prepare that. Any format constraints?
[09:48] Ravi Patel: CSV with columns: request_id, timestamp, tokens, route_tag, streaming_flag. Use the same IDs as in your app logs so we can correlate.
[09:58] Daniel Kim: Noted.
[10:00] Camila Ortiz: We'll also include our KV telemetry schema and a link to the benchmark-matrix for interpretation.
[10:06] (typing)
[10:10] Tomoko Sato: Regarding the compressed KV option — can you share expected p95 delta?
[10:15] Ravi Patel: In our tests compressed KV reduces p95 under memory pressure by ~20-30% because it halves page size; decode overhead adds ~5-10ms per page-in. We'll include microbenchmarks specific to your trace.
[10:27] Lina Alvarez: Sounds promising.
[10:30] Daniel Kim: Anything else we should be aware of re: routing? For example sticky sessions?
[10:34] Ravi Patel: Sticky sessions help if session reuse is high; they reduce cross-worker prefix reuse loss. But they reduce global pooling efficiency. Another knob is request-affinity by user or session id for a subset.
[10:47] Camila Ortiz: Let's recap next steps. Ravi?
[10:50] Ravi Patel: Sure. Action items: I'll run eviction replay with your trace, sweep kv-page-size and prefetch-window, test compressed KV, and produce a short results doc. Camila will send configs and telemetry schema. Daniel and team will provide enriched trace and confirm pilot routing split.
[11:10] Daniel Kim: We'll get the trace and session IDs by EOD Tuesday.
[11:14] Tomoko Sato: And we'll confirm whether Private is preferred or if Dedicated is acceptable for pilot.
[11:18] Camila Ortiz: Great. I'll follow up with the deck and sample YAML.
[11:22] (short closing)
[11:25] Camila Ortiz: Thanks everyone. We'll sync next week after Ravi posts the replay results.

Notes on transcription quirks: occasional mis-heard named entities (Redwood runtime sometimes transcribed as "Red Wood runtime"), filler words, and minor speaker attribution swaps early in the call. Some audio drop at 00:20 caused a missing 3s segment.

End of transcript.
